title: Naive Bayes Classifier

blocks.t: From the notes
Naive Bayes, as written
Based on Bayes' theorem:
P(C | X) = \frac{P(X | C) P(C)}{P(X)}
posterior $=\dfrac{\textbf{likelihood}\times\textbf{prior}}{\textbf{evidence}}$

It is called naive because it assumes all the features are
independent of each other, which is rarely true in real life.

$P(X)$ is the same for every class, so we can ignore the
denominator and just compare numerators.

Very fast, works very well for text classification — spam
filtering, sentiment analysis.

blocks.cap:
Left: the theorem and the assumption. Middle: what GaussianNB actually
estimates — one mean and one variance per feature per class. Right: the
resulting boundary is quadratic when per-class variances differ.

blocks.t: Derivation
We want the most probable class given the evidence:

\hat c = \arg\max_{c} P(C=c \mid x_1,\dots,x_d)
 = \arg\max_{c} \frac{P(x_1,\dots,x_d \mid c) P(c)}{P(x_1,\dots,x_d)} .
The denominator does not depend on $c$, so
\hat c = \arg\max_c P(x_1,\dots,x_d\mid c) P(c).

The joint likelihood $P(x_1,\dots,x_d\mid c)$ is the problem. By the chain rule
it is $P(x_1|c)P(x_2|x_1,c)\cdots P(x_d|x_1..x_{d-1},c)$ — for $d$ binary
features that is $2^d-1$ parameters per class, which is unlearnable.

The naive assumption — conditional independence given the class —
collapses it:
P(x_1,\dots,x_d \mid c) = \prod_{j=1}^{d} P(x_j \mid c),
reducing the count from exponential to $d$ parameters per class. Hence
\boxed{ \hat c=\arg\max_c \log P(c)+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\log P(x_j\mid c) }

where we take logs because multiplying hundreds of small probabilities
underflows to exactly $0.0$ in floating point.

Conditional independence is not independence. The assumption is that
features are independent once you know the class — "free" and
"money" may be strongly correlated overall, but the claim is that within spam
emails alone, knowing one tells you nothing about the other. That is a much
weaker claim than plain independence, though still usually false.
Why it works despite being wrong
The key insight

Naive Bayes only has to get the arg-max right, not the probabilities.
The independence assumption ruins the magnitude of the posterior — it
double-counts correlated evidence, pushing estimates towards 0 or 1 — but it
frequently preserves the ordering of the classes.

Zhang (2004) made this precise: the dependencies between features often
distribute evenly across classes and cancel out in the comparison. So a model
whose probability estimates are badly wrong can still classify correctly.

The practical reading: trust predict, distrust
predict_proba. If you need honest probabilities, wrap it in
CalibratedClassifierCV.

blocks.cap:
Left: as features become redundant, NB degrades while logistic
regression does not — correlated evidence gets counted twice. Middle: Laplace
smoothing rescues zero counts. Right: NB's probabilities are pushed to the
extremes; the ranking survives, the calibration does not.

blocks.t: A worked spam example

Priors: $P(\text{spam})=0.40$, $P(\text{ham})=0.60$.
Likelihoods from the counts:
P(\text{free}|S)=\tfrac{32}{40}=0.80,\quad P(\text{meeting}|S)=\tfrac{2}{40}=0.05,
P(\text{free}|H)=\tfrac{6}{60}=0.10,\quad P(\text{meeting}|H)=\tfrac{30}{60}=0.50 .
A mail containing both words:

\text{score}(S)=0.40\times0.80\times0.05=0.0160,\qquad
\text{score}(H)=0.60\times0.10\times0.50=0.0300 .

Normalising: $P(S|x)=\frac{0.016}{0.016+0.030}=\mathbf{0.348}$ — classified
ham.

Now suppose "lottery" never appeared in any ham mail: $P(\text{lottery}|H)=0$.
Then every product involving it is zero, and a single unseen word vetoes
the entire class regardless of all other evidence. Laplace smoothing with
$\alpha$ fixes this:
P(w\mid c)=\frac{\text{count}(w,c)+\alpha}{\displaystyle\sum_{w'}\text{count}(w',c)+\alpha |V|} .

With $\alpha=1$ every word gets a small nonzero probability, and no single term
can veto a class. $\alpha$ is a smoothing prior — it is Bayesian shrinkage
towards a uniform distribution over the vocabulary.
The four variants

head: Variant
Assumed $P(x_j|c)$
Use it when
rows: Continuous features. Estimates two numbers per feature per class. No $\alpha$; var_smoothing instead.
Word/term counts or TF-IDF. The classic text model. Features must be non-negative.
Binary presence/absence. Explicitly penalises words that are absent — better on short documents.
Imbalanced text. Estimates each class's parameters from all other classes, which stabilises rare classes.

A synthetic four-topic corpus. Left: accuracy of the three text

blocks.t:
Why NB is so good at text. Documents live in a space with tens of
thousands of dimensions and each one is extremely sparse. Estimating
correlations there is hopeless with realistic amounts of data, so the naive
assumption costs less than the variance it saves. On top of that, training is
one pass of counting — $O(nd_{\text{nonzero}})$ with no iteration — so it
scales to corpora that would choke an iterative model, and it supports
partial_fit for streaming.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.naive_bayes import (GaussianNB, MultinomialNB,
                                 BernoulliNB, ComplementNB)
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification, load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV, cross_val_score
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer, TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, brier_score_loss

# ==================================================================
# 1. GAUSSIAN NAIVE BAYES FROM SCRATCH -- fit is just mean and variance
# ==================================================================
class MyGaussianNB:
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.classes_ = np.unique(y)
        self.prior_ = np.array([(y == c).mean() for c in self.classes_])
        self.mu_    = np.array([X[y == c].mean(axis=0) for c in self.classes_])
        self.var_   = np.array([X[y == c].var(axis=0) + 1e-9
                                for c in self.classes_])
        return self

    def _log_likelihood(self, X):
        # log N(x | mu, var), summed over features -- the naive product in logs
        out = []
        for k in range(len(self.classes_)):
            ll = -0.5 * (np.log(2 * np.pi * self.var_[k])
                         + (X - self.mu_[k]) ** 2 / self.var_[k])
            out.append(ll.sum(axis=1) + np.log(self.prior_[k]))
        return np.array(out).T                       # (n, n_classes)

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.classes_[self._log_likelihood(X).argmax(axis=1)]

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        L = self._log_likelihood(X)
        L -= L.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)            # log-sum-exp for stability
        P = np.exp(L)
        return P / P.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

iris = load_iris()
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(iris.data, iris.target,
                                      test_size=0.3, stratify=iris.target,
                                      random_state=0)
print("scratch:", (MyGaussianNB().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte) == yte).mean())
print("sklearn:", GaussianNB().fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte))

# What the model actually stores -- 2 numbers per feature per class. That's it.
g = GaussianNB().fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("theta_ (means)  shape:", g.theta_.shape)
print("var_            shape:", g.var_.shape)
print("class_prior_          :", g.class_prior_.round(3))

# ==================================================================
# 2. TEXT: the classic use case
# ==================================================================
docs = ["win money now free lottery",  "meeting at ten tomorrow",
        "free free cash prize claim",  "project deadline meeting notes",
        "claim your free prize now",   "lunch meeting with the team"]
labels = [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0]            # 1 = spam

# CountVectorizer -> MultinomialNB is the textbook pipeline
spam = make_pipeline(CountVectorizer(), MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0)).fit(docs, labels)
print(spam.predict(["free money claim now", "team meeting notes"]))

# Inspect the learned log-likelihoods -- feature_log_prob_ is log P(word | class)
vec = spam.named_steps["countvectorizer"]
nb  = spam.named_steps["multinomialnb"]
words = np.array(vec.get_feature_names_out())
spammy = words[np.argsort(nb.feature_log_prob_[1] - nb.feature_log_prob_[0])[-4:]]
print("most spam-indicative words:", spammy)

# ==================================================================
# 3. TUNING alpha -- usually the ONLY hyperparameter
# ==================================================================
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=3000, n_features=200, n_informative=40,
                           n_classes=4, n_clusters_per_class=1, random_state=0)
Xc = np.abs(X)                            # MultinomialNB needs non-negative
gs = GridSearchCV(MultinomialNB(),
                  {"alpha": [1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0, 20.0]},
                  cv=5, n_jobs=4).fit(Xc, y)
print("best alpha:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# alpha=0 is MLE and will produce -inf logs for unseen combinations.
# alpha=1 is Laplace/add-one; alpha<1 is Lidstone and often better for text.

# ==================================================================
# 4. THE VARIANTS COMPARED ON THE SAME COUNTS
# ==================================================================
corpus = ["a b c a", "b b d", "c c c a", "d d e", "a e e b", "c d e a"]
target = [0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0]
counts = CountVectorizer().fit_transform(corpus)
for M in (MultinomialNB, BernoulliNB, ComplementNB):
    print(M.__name__, round(cross_val_score(M(alpha=0.5), counts, target,
                                            cv=3).mean(), 3))

# BernoulliNB binarises internally (binarize=0.0 by default). It uses the
# ABSENCE of a word as evidence too, which Multinomial ignores entirely.

# ==================================================================
# 5. CALIBRATION -- NB ranks well but its probabilities are extreme
# ==================================================================
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=4000, n_features=20, n_informative=8,
                           n_redundant=6, random_state=0)   # redundancy hurts NB
Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.4, random_state=0)

raw = GaussianNB().fit(Xa, ya)
cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(GaussianNB(), method="isotonic", cv=5).fit(Xa, ya)
print("raw  Brier:", round(brier_score_loss(yb, raw.predict_proba(Xb)[:, 1]), 4))
print("cal  Brier:", round(brier_score_loss(yb, cal.predict_proba(Xb)[:, 1]), 4))
# Accuracy barely moves; the probabilities become usable.

# ==================================================================
# 6. STREAMING -- partial_fit for data that does not fit in memory
# ==================================================================
stream = MultinomialNB(alpha=0.5)
classes = np.unique(y)
for start in range(0, 4000, 500):
    chunk = np.abs(X[start:start + 500])
    stream.partial_fit(chunk, y[start:start + 500], classes=classes)
print("streamed model trained on 8 chunks:", round(stream.score(np.abs(X), y), 4))
Everything on one page
Summary

Rule: $\hat c=\arg\max_c \big[\log P(c)+\sum_j \log P(x_j\mid c)\big]$.
Drop $P(X)$ — it is constant across classes. Use logs — products of many
small probabilities underflow.

The naive assumption is conditional independence given the class. It
turns $2^d$ parameters into $d$ per class. It is nearly always false and often
harmless, because only the arg-max must survive.

Laplace smoothing $\alpha$ stops a single unseen feature value from
zeroing out an entire class. It is usually the only hyperparameter.

Variants: Gaussian (continuous), Multinomial (counts/TF-IDF),
Bernoulli (binary presence, uses absence as evidence), Complement (imbalanced
text).

Weaknesses: correlated/redundant features double-count evidence and
degrade accuracy; probabilities are badly calibrated (over-confident); cannot
learn feature interactions — XOR is impossible; GaussianNB assumes normality
per feature per class.

Rules of thumb: remove or merge highly correlated features; use
$\alpha<1$ for text; calibrate if you need probabilities; always run it first
as the baseline before reaching for anything complicated.
Interview corner
Q. What is "naive" about Naive Bayes?

The assumption that features are conditionally independent given the class:
$P(x_1,\dots,x_d|c)=\prod_j P(x_j|c)$. It reduces the parameter count from
exponential to linear in $d$, at the price of an assumption that is usually
false.
Q. Why can we ignore the denominator $P(X)$?

It is the same for every class, so it cannot change which class maximises the
posterior. We do need it if we want normalised probabilities, and it is
recovered by dividing by the sum of the class scores.
Q. Why does it work when the assumption is violated?

Classification only requires the correct arg-max. Dependency effects often
inflate all class scores in a similar way and cancel in the comparison. The
probability magnitudes are wrong; the ranking frequently is not.
Q. What is the zero-frequency problem?

If a feature value never co-occurs with a class in training, its estimated
likelihood is 0 and the whole product collapses to 0, vetoing that class. Fixed
by Laplace/Lidstone smoothing: add $\alpha$ to every count and $\alpha|V|$ to
the denominator.
Q. Why work in log space?

Multiplying thousands of probabilities each around $10^{-4}$ underflows to
exactly zero in float64. Logs turn the product into a sum, which is numerically
stable; converting back to probabilities uses log-sum-exp.
Q. Multinomial vs Bernoulli for text?

Multinomial models how many times each word occurs and ignores absent
words. Bernoulli models presence/absence and explicitly uses the absence of a
word as evidence. Bernoulli tends to win on short documents (tweets, subject
lines); Multinomial on longer ones.
Q. Is Naive Bayes a linear classifier?

Multinomial and Bernoulli NB are: the log-posterior is linear in the counts, so
the boundary is a hyperplane. GaussianNB is linear only if the per-class
variances are equal; otherwise the quadratic terms survive and the boundary is
a conic.
Q. Naive Bayes vs logistic regression?

They are a generative/discriminative pair over the same model family. NB models
$P(x|c)P(c)$ and solves in closed form from counts; logistic regression models
$P(c|x)$ directly and optimises it. Ng and Jordan showed NB reaches its
(higher) asymptotic error much faster, so it wins with little data while
logistic regression wins with plenty.
Q. Can Naive Bayes learn XOR?

No. Each feature contributes an independent additive term to the log-posterior,
so the model is additive and cannot represent an interaction where the effect of
$x_1$ depends on $x_2$. You would have to engineer the interaction feature
yourself.
Q. How would you improve a Naive Bayes text classifier?

Tune $\alpha$; use TF-IDF instead of raw counts; add bigrams; remove or merge
near-duplicate features to reduce double-counting; use ComplementNB if the
classes are imbalanced; and calibrate the output if downstream code consumes
probabilities.
